title: Majors, minors, and exotics

inOneLine.simple: Pairs are grouped by how widely traded their currencies are, which affects their costs.

explain.simple: Major pairs contain the US dollar and one other widely traded currency, such as EUR/USD, USD/JPY, or GBP/USD. Minor pairs (also called crosses) pair two major currencies without the dollar, such as EUR/GBP or EUR/JPY. Exotic pairs pair a major currency with the currency of a smaller or emerging economy, such as USD/ZAR or USD/TRY. Exotics usually trade less, so their [[spread|spreads]] tend to be wider and prices can jump more.
explain.balanced: The common classification: majors are USD paired with EUR, JPY, GBP, CHF, AUD, CAD, or NZD. Crosses (minors) combine those currencies without USD. Exotics include an emerging-market or less-traded currency. Lower [[liquidity]] usually means wider spreads, larger gaps, and higher swap costs. Exact groupings vary between brokers.

assumptions: An exotic pair with a spread of 60 pips
steps: Opening and immediately closing EUR/USD costs about 1 pip.
Doing the same on the exotic pair costs about 60 pips.
Before a trade on the exotic even breaks even, price must move 60 times further in your favour than on EUR/USD.

assumptions: Classify each pair using the definitions above
steps: USD/CAD: major (dollar plus a major currency).
EUR/JPY: minor or cross (two majors, no dollar).

explainSimpler: Majors include the dollar, minors leave the dollar out, and exotics include a less-traded currency that usually costs more to trade.
commonMistake: Assuming every pair costs the same to trade. Always check the spread before you practise on a pair, especially exotics.

quickCheck.prompt: Why do exotic pairs usually have wider spreads?

options.text: They are usually traded less, so liquidity is lower
options.explanation: Right: fewer buyers and sellers usually means a wider gap between bid and ask.

options.text: They are newer pairs, so brokers have not settled their spreads yet
options.explanation: No: spreads reflect how much trading there is, not how new a pair is. Fewer buyers and sellers usually means a wider gap.

options.text: They are only traded at night
options.explanation: No: exotic pairs can be traded whenever the market is open. The wider spread comes from lower liquidity.

doItNow.instructions: In MetaTrader on your demo account, open the quotes list and add 5 pairs: 3 majors, 1 minor, and 1 exotic. Note each pair's spread.

homework: Check the spread on EUR/USD and on your exotic pair at two different times of day, and write both down.
